Atlanta Fed GDPNow’s final Q3 nowcast came in at 3.27% Wednesday, the least since it initiated tracking for the quarter and down from its 6.18% peak on August 3. Q3 GDP is out later this morning.

How much weight to put on it? Over the past two years its last reading before GDP has been either very close or well off, with little in between:

▪ Within a tenth in 4 of the last 8 quarters (Q3 & Q4 ‘24, Q2 ‘25, Q2 ‘26)
▪ Off 0.75 pt or more in the other 4, two of them (Q4 ‘25 & Q1 ‘26) mostly from the federal shutdown
▪ Since 2014 (ex-2020), its average miss is 0.59 pt: within half a point half the time, within a point 84% of the time

Two tendencies worth noting for today:
▪ When GDPNow falls more than half a point in the final month (it’s down 1.75 pts from 5.02% on Sept 25), the actual print has come in above its final reading in 16 of 22 quarters
▪ In third quarters specifically, the print has come in above GDPNow’s final reading in 10 of 14 quarters (ex-2020), by an average of 0.31 pt

This quarter it has company: as of Friday, six of the seven major GDP trackers I follow were between 3.1% and 3.7%, with the NY Fed the outlier at 2.67%. All seven are well above the Blue Chip consensus of ~2.5%.

I mentioned the October rate hike call from BofA was curious.  So where did they pivot to?

BofA’s Bhave (senior US Economist) called it “a not-so-hawkish hold.” Warsh pointed to tighter financial conditions as a sign the September hike is working and wouldn’t lean into a December move, which BofA calls dovish since markets are pricing one.

BofA’s rates strategist Mark Cabana says the bond market didn’t see Warsh as credible on inflation:

▪ From the start of the press conference, the 2-year yield fell 6 bp and the 30-year rose 4 bp. That steepening was bigger than BofA’s 5–7 bp ballpark and not far from July’s 12.5 bp
▪ The dollar fell 0.2%–0.3%, about half its July drop
▪ December hike pricing slipped to 21 bp from 23 bp

BofA now expects hikes in December and March, with its 4.25%–4.50% terminal rate unchanged. It warns the long end will “continue to haunt” the Fed until it gets more serious on inflation, and says the move raises the odds Treasury trims long-end auction sizes at the Nov. 4 refunding.

From the @dailychartbook nightly email comes a JPMorgan chart via the great @LJKawa, with the accompanying note arguing that with above-trend EPS growth (~15% y/y), "10yr yields can continue to rise to ~5% before the equity multiple starts to de-rate," and if strong growth projections are realized, equities "should be able to withstand a 10yr yield level closer to ~5.5-6.0%."  

2026 looks like it will easily land on the "hyper-growth" curve (>20% EPS growth), currently estimated at +32.8% per FactSet.  

But 2027 EPS growth is a different story currently estimated at +16% per FactSet. That puts it on the above-trend curve, where the note puts de-rating at ~5%. With the 10-yr at 5.04%, on 2027 earnings we're already at the edge of the tolerance, not 50-100 bp away from it.  

The bigger takeaway from JPM's chart though might be that at 5%, dropping one growth regime costs ~4 turns of P/E (about -17%), while another 100 bp within a regime costs just ~0.5 turn (my read of their curves). That argues for watching the E, not the yield.  

But does the multiple already discount it? FactSet's forward P/E is 18.7x, below its 5- and 10-yr averages, so it looks priced for above-trend, not hyper, growth.

Bloomberg: America’s closest allies have nearly stopped buying Treasuries.

According to Bloomberg's analysis, countries that vote most often with the U.S. at the U.N. bought a net $174.3B of Treasury notes and bonds in January through August. That’s the least for the period since 2021, and down more than 60% from a year earlier.

▪️ Japan, the biggest foreign holder, bought just $389M, down 99%
▪️ South Korea sold $23.8B, its biggest January–August sale in records going back to 1977
▪️ Taiwan also sold more than it bought
▪️ Countries that vote least often with the U.S. bought $17.1B, ending four straight years of selling. China is still the biggest seller.

Hedge funds, banks and other private investors have filled the gap and now hold about 70% of federal debt. But they’re more sensitive to price.

State Street’s Masahiko Loo: the market “isn’t losing foreign buyers — it’s losing automatic buyers.”

This week’s auctions showed some other evidence. Indirect bidders, often used as a stand-in for foreign demand, took 45.7% of Monday’s 2-year (vs. a 58.3% average) and 60.1% of Tuesday’s 5-year (vs. 64%). The 7-year sells Thursday.

Have them bring the work product back and then make sure that they didn’t just give a prompt to the model.

Those kids need to be good at using them, and they also just need to be taught that they can do anything."

The U.S. Treasury market alone is worth $31.8T.

Meanwhile, tokenized U.S. Treasury products onchain account for just $14.5B.

DeFi offers exposure to other traditional assets, but only a tiny fraction of these markets is represented onchain so far.

Take @apyx_fi, for example: Its apyUSD earns from Strategy's preferred-share dividends, while aptUSD earns from U.S. Treasuries.

Let's see what each one offers and how they compare ↓

1. apyUSD

Let's start with @Strategy.

Besides buying Bitcoin, the company also issues $STRC, a type of preferred share that pays regular cash dividends.

Apyx uses these shares to back apxUSD, its dollar token. Users can then deposit apxUSD to receive apyUSD and earn from those dividends.

Here's what apyUSD offers:

→ Yield source: STRC preferred-share dividends
→ Recent yield: 13.77% (annualized over 30 days)
→ Withdrawals: 3-20 days

The process is pretty simple - you deposit apxUSD, receive apyUSD, and its value gradually grows relative to apxUSD as yield accumulates.

If we assume STRC returns to its $100 par value, the yield can go as high as 16.07%.

Personally, I'd consider this for capital I don't plan to withdraw anytime soon.

2. aptUSD

For those who prefer easier access to their funds, aptUSD offers another option.

It's backed by U.S. Treasuries and cash equivalents, with a different set of conditions:

→ Yield source: U.S. Treasuries and cash equivalents
→ Current yield: Around 3.5% APY
→ Withdrawals: No lockup or cooldown

You hold aptUSD, and the yield accumulates automatically without needing to stake or deposit it anywhere else.

The yield is obviously lower than apyUSD, but you get more flexibility and confidence with your funds.

3. Bigger Vision

@apyx_fi plans to bring more traditional sources of income into DeFi, beyond preferred shares and Treasuries.

They've already made some progress:

→ Four completed security audits
→ apxUSD listed on Kraken
→ Products across Ethereum, Base, BNB Chain, and Solana

As the platform expands, $APYX is intended to play a bigger role.

The token has a fixed supply of 100M and will let holders vote on protocol decisions.

There are also plans to distribute 50% of monthly reserve growth to $APYX stakers, with the other half staying in the protocol's reserves.

Token holders can benefit as reserves grow, while the protocol keeps building up the assets supporting its products.

IMO, they've struck a nice balance here.

4. My Take

If you think about it, Apyx already lets you earn income tied to Strategy's preferred shares or U.S. government debt, all through DeFi.

Those are two completely different corners of traditional finance.

Imagine being able to build an entire income portfolio across five or ten different markets, without needing a traditional brokerage account.

I'd happily spend time comparing which assets are paying me, what risks I'm taking, and how much of my money I want exposed to each.

That's my kind of homework ٩(◕‿◕)۶

This month @Deloitte published “Five Trends Shaping Marketing in 2026”.

Here’s the TL;DR ↓

1. Budget pressure is rising: shorter horizons, tighter spend, more CFO scrutiny, and tougher ROI demands.

2. Consumers are more selective and cutting non-essentials, but will still pay more when the value feels clear.

3. Customer experience is becoming a bigger differentiator, and discovery is shifting beyond search to social, creators, communities, and recommendations.

4. AI can lower content costs, speed production, and improve personalisation – but trust is shaky.

5. Most firms are investing more in AI, yet big returns from agentic AI are still rare. Value often takes years and depends on systems, governance, and operating model – not tools alone.

My reading:

2026 is probably the year when everything that used to work in marketing suddenly stopped working – attribution broke, and ROAS started falling across key acquisition channels.

If I had to share my 5 marketing projections for 2027, they’d be:

• More experimentation with AI optimisation; a race for recommendations and citations

• A marketing-budget crisis – and increased demand for evidence-based marketing

• A new rise of guerrilla and situational marketing

• Trust/brand become economic assets

• AI becomes part of marketing workflows; teams that ignore AI underperform and get fired

What are yours?

🇫🇷 France now borrows at higher rates than Italy, its 10-year bond yield has exceeded 5% while its sovereign risk premium has returned to levels reminiscent of the eurozone debt crisis. Is France becoming the next Greece? The real danger seems elsewhere.

📈 I don't believe France is heading toward a Greek-style solvency crisis but rather a crisis of fiscal credibility that could become concerning. With public debt approaching 120% of GDP, a fiscal deficit expected to reach 5.4% this year and weak potential growth, France is entering a dangerous dynamic. Investors are questioning its ability to stabilize public finances, demanding higher yields, which progressively increases debt-servicing costs and makes deficit reduction even harder. The average maturity of French debt, exceeding eight years, slows the transmission of higher interest rates but it doesn't eliminate the problem.

🇬🇷 The comparison with Greece is quite misleading. Unlike them in 2009, France has a diversified economy, a relatively balanced current account and a resilient banking system. However, with €3.6 trillion in public debt, France represents a far greater systemic risk to Europe. A prolonged deterioration in French sovereign creditworthiness could affect banks, credit markets and financing conditions across the eurozone.

🏦 The fundamental problem is political. With public spending close to 57% of GDP and an already exceptionally high tax burden, France has limited room for maneuver. Continuing to postpone structural adjustments means allowing markets to impose their own discipline through higher borrowing costs. So I believe we are witnessing a persistently elevated sovereign risk premium rather than an imminent default.

⚠️ France's greatest risk is more a self-reinforcing cycle of economic and fiscal stagnation. A country that continues servicing its debt but devotes its resources to interest payments rather than investment, productivity and future growth. A gradual decline can last for decades without triggering any meaningful political response.

How long markets will continue financing a fiscal trajectory that its political leaders can no longer credibly defend ? This is the main question.

My core focus here is purely on price given this is a reflection of all market views and collective action. So how I am thinking is the following:

> I distinctively remember an excellent trader saying 'people would be much better off if they traded the 1M chart instead of LTF'. If we are to view the 1Y/1M it's evident we are in a range between 2025 lows and highs with a concrete 1M reclaim occurring in August 26.

> 2025 lows are sitting at $74.3K and remain a core invalidation level if we see a monthly close below this level. Equally on 1M there is a supply order block starting at $83K which thus far has provided resistance for price. > As per with any range low reclaim you want to be looking to long a rest of the lows and aiming towards the mid range atleast. Therefore, think any dips towards high 70s targeting 96-104K would be the next trade thats on the table.

> If this idea were to be invalidated there would be earlier signs that emerge being the 1W 50 SMA cracking and price trading below there for a considerable duration. The longer price trades above the 1W 50 SMA the stronger my conviction the idea will not be invalidated.

Any price action inbetween to me is irrelevant. I understand people trade much lower timeframes than I do and on leverage. What I am watching purely is the monthly closes and my outlined levels. If these levels are not invalidated then I only see the need to be patient. 

In summary, high to mid 70s remain attractive, no invalidation has occurred on the 1M and looks to be an accumulation phase after breaking above key levels until proven otherwise.

As a follow-up,

While the chairman is not offering forward guidance, other FOMC members are.

In particular, New York Fed President John Williams and Vice Chairman Philip Jefferson offered the forward guidance to the Fed holding at this meeting earlier this month. Before that, it was Fed Governor Chris Waller that was offering forward guidance (leading into the hike in September)

So another thing the Fed should ditch, or radically shorten, is its self-imposed blackout period of not talking in public. 

This made sense when everybody was supposed to clear the way for the chairman to speak because he was the voice that spoke for the committee. 

That's no longer the case, as this is a very independent committee with, as Warsh repeatedly said yesterday, "sobering discussions," "family fights," and with one meeting to go, more dissenting votes against the majority than any year since 1982. 

Now the real forward guidance doesn't start until tomorrow, when that blackout is lifted 48 hours after the FOMC meeting, and the other 18 FOMC  members tell us what they think.

We've inverted Fed communication.

The least important voice now is the chairman because he's not offering forward guidance. The more important voices, at least for now, are everybody else that is offering forward guidance and presumably had their speeches vetted and approved by the Federal Reserve.

re: the “communist/socialist” boogeyman in America

what’s interesting is you see a lot of Republican candidates pushing this messaging as a way to discredit Democratic challengers in races across the country (especially at the national level)

but it’s not really detracting from their appeal anymore. why?

the terms communism, socialism, etc. had much greater relevance to people in prior decades due to the Soviet threat. everyone associated communism with the USSR. and there was very little integration and trade between the US and USSR

but ofc, the USSR no longer exists. so what about China? aren’t they communist?

sort of, but to people sitting in the US, China actually comes across as hyper-capitalist (albeit authoritarian), especially on the global stage. i.e., people buy a ton of Chinese products (knowingly and unknowingly) and know that they are now maybe the greatest physically productive nation on the planet today

so the terms “communist” and “socialist” don’t have the same negative connotation they once had. we’re a full generation past the collapse of the USSR. and the one great power which is called “communist” seems to not be collapsing under its own weight

combine this with the specter of AI-related job losses and you can see why these ideologies are becoming more appealing to more people, especially when people can see that the government is increasingly corrupt and their cost of living is getting much worse relative to their wages

i don’t think socialism as it’s conceived of by organizations such as the DSA is the answer at all, but you’d have to be blind not to see that we need revisions to our economic model if it cannot sustain a thriving middle class of workers (especially in the face of greater destruction of that middle class through AI). even Elon seems to acknowledge this by talking about “universal high income”

the longer it takes us to start having these discussions, the more calamitous it will be once the boiling point is reached

anyway, don’t shoot the messenger…

People were writing off Bitcoin's network. Well, the compute is coming back on.

Hash rate (14d avg) dropped 23% from the Oct record into Feb, deepest fall since the 2021 China ban. Part of that was a winter storm, but the story that stuck was miners leaving for AI. It bounced, then slid again into July.

- Security. Every exahash makes attacking Bitcoin more expensive.
- Conviction. Miners are adding on razor thin margins.
- Energy. Mining is a flexible load grids can switch off when needed.

North star metric for me. Since my BI days my go-to on mining and energy grids has been @DSBatten. Follow his work.

Every score comes from a published investigation of an extraction operation: a rug, a bundled launch, an insider dump, a serial deployer. Every investigation is based on onchain evidence. No investigation, no score.

Why a wallet gets marked: the investigation shows it took part in the extraction. It deployed, bundled, sniped, dumped, funded the operation or collected the proceeds.

Never marked: victims, buyers who lost money, exchanges, DEXs, bots and other infrastructure, and early traders we can show acted on their own. Touching a rugged coin is not enough.

Side wallets: when we can prove one person or group controls several wallets, the record follows them across all of them.

What raises a score:
• Repeat offending. Each separate operation counts more than one big one.
• Role. Running the operation counts more than a supporting wallet.
• Serial launching. The more launches, the higher.
• Size of the extraction. from under $10K (least) up to $10M+ (most).
• Recency. Old cases fade, unless the operator is still launching. People are automatically forgiven for past Crime, unless they keep their bad behavior
